speaker: gm
text:
A grey-coated clerk turns slowly from the sack hoist above the shut loft door. A pigeon occupies the beam above him, apparently satisfied with its position in public life. Below, a scrawny boy in enormous boots lobs gutter stones at the body. On the wall, a sharp-faced girl swears at the yard in Common and something saltier.

A woman in a rain cape steps away from the open gate, notebook in hand. “Sergeant Agnes Kell. The Captain calls it suicide. I reserve judgement.” A stone clangs off the hoist hook. The boy looks up at the sound; the pigeon does not.

speaker: player
text: Corvin Vale, at the King's pleasure, Sergeant. Reserved judgement is the most valuable kind; I'd like to buy some of yours. (I flip a copper toward the boy in the big boots.) And you, young sir, that copper's yours if you stop stoning the dead man and tell me what you saw this morning.

speaker: gm
text:
The copper arcs towards the boy. He catches it against his waistcoat, then closes his fist around it.

“Cob found ’em. Cob don’t talk cheap, neither. Porters found Mister Prout when it got light. Cob ain’t scared of a dead man.”

“Shut it, Cob.”

“Cob can talk if Cob’s paid. That’s talking. You got your copper’s worth.”

The girl’s heels stop drumming the wall. Kell makes a short note without looking up.

“Payment to a witness. Noted.”

marks.note: You offered Cob a copper for what he saw, and he’s making clear that’s why he’s talking.

speaker: player
text: (I crouch to Cob's height and lower my voice.) Cob, a man who doesn't talk cheap is a man after my own heart. You said Cob found 'em. Found what, exactly? There's a silver in it if it's something the porters didn't see.

speaker: gm
text:
Cob’s eyes follow the silver, then the big boots planted on his feet. He pockets the copper you already gave him and grins as if he’s just completed a sound piece of business.

“Cob found the boots. They’re Cob’s. And Cob sleeps where Cob likes.”

“Shut it, Cob.”

“Cob ain’t scared of no dead man, neither. Porters found him when it got light. That’s worth a silver, easy.”

The girl’s gaze flicks to the coin in your hand, then back to Cob. Her heels start drumming the wall again. Kell writes in her notebook.

“Payment offered for information. Noted.”

speaker: player
text: (I keep the silver between two fingers and glance up at the hanging clerk's feet.) Fine boots, Cob. Better than the porters wear. Clerk's size, I'd say. Where did they come off him, and when? Tell me true and this silver's yours, and nobody's taking the boots.

speaker: gm
text:
Cob looks from the silver to his boots. His grin turns calculating.

“For a look? A silver’s for looking at both. Two if you want Cob to take one off. They’re Cob’s, mind.”

He shoves the offered coin away with the toe of an oversized boot, then stamps once. The left one gives a faint crackle.

“Hear that? Fine boots. Don’t go poking at ’em.”

The girl in the shawl’s heels stop against the wall. “Boots: claimed by the boy. Coin: offered for inspection. Noted.”

marks.note: You offered a silver for the boots’ story, and Cob is bargaining for a higher price to let you inspect them.

speaker: player
text: (I laugh and count two silver into my palm.) You drive a hard bargain, Cob, I respect it. Two silver, the left boot off, just for a look, and it goes straight back on your foot after. Sergeant, witness that the boots stay his.

speaker: gm
text:
Kell looks from the two silver coins to Cob. Her pencil pauses above the notebook.

“The boots stay his. I witness that.”

Cob’s eyes fix on the coins. He stops throwing stones and plants both feet squarely on the cobbles.

“Two silver, for a look. Not for taking. Cob’s boots stay on Cob.”

He tucks the coins into his waistcoat, then folds his arms over the boots as though their ownership might need defending from the weather.

“There. You’ve looked. Fine boots.”

speaker: player
text: (I tilt my head, still smiling.) Cob. The deal was the left boot off. You named the price yourself, and a man who welshes on his own price never gets a second deal in this city. (I turn to the girl on the wall.) Miss, you seem the sensible one. Does Cob keep his word, or do I take my business to you?

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to get Cob to take off his left boot for a look: 20 + 6 = 26 vs DC 15: success (natural 20!)

speaker: gm
text:
Cob scowls at your smile, then sits on the water butt and unlaces his left boot.

“Just a look. Boot stays Cob’s.”

The left boot comes off. Inside its lining, a folded, stiff page is sewn in with small neat stitches. Cob takes the boot straight back and begins tugging it on again.

The page lists grain wagons marked “lost to goblins,” each countersigned “J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor.” Beside each entry, Prout has pencilled what the same wagon weighed at the river warehouses two days later. At the bottom: “Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?”

Kell reads over your shoulder. She goes very still.

“He came to me three days ago. Asked how to report false entries in the King’s rolls. I told him to take it to the palace.” She looks at the page. “I should have listened.”

marks.note: You promised the boot would go straight back on his foot, and Cob is holding you to the deal’s limits.

speaker: player
text: (Quietly, to Kell, keeping my back to the yard.) Then let's listen now. Who is J. Sallow, Sergeant, and where does the Royal Purveyor keep his office? (A little louder, to Cob.) And Cob: one more silver for the page itself. The boot's yours; the paper's a dead man's letter, and it ought to reach the King.

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to buy the page from Cob: 13 + 6 = 19 vs DC 18: success

speaker: gm
text:
Cob pockets one silver and hands you the folded page. The boot stays on his foot.

“Cob keeps the boot. That was the bargain.”

Kell answers without taking her eyes off the page. She has heard you offer Cob silver before; now her pencil rests against the notebook as if it is weighing the difference.

“J. Sallow. Under-purveyor for grain. I know the signature from the Assembly delivery notices. I’ve never seen the man. The Purveyor’s office is in the palace back courts.” She glances up. “That’s all I know of him, investigator.”

marks.note: The Royal Purveyor’s office handles the palace’s supplies, including grain. Its offices are in the palace’s back courts.

speaker: player
text: (I tuck the page inside my doublet and stroll to the foot of the wall, looking up at the girl.) That second language of yours, miss, it wasn't Halfling and it wasn't Dwarvish. Hedge-folk talk, I'd wager. A clever girl who speaks goblin and sits on granary walls hears things. What's your price for who was in this yard last night?

speaker: gm
text:
The girl’s mouth twists. Her fist stays shut.

“Goblin? That’s a new one. You want to buy a story, ask the boy. I’ve already sold mine.”

Cob looks up sharply at “Sallow.” The stones stop moving in his hands. Kell’s pencil taps once against her notebook.

“The page puts the wagons and Sallow’s signature together. It does not put him in this yard last night, or say how Prout died.” Her eyes lift to yours. “What’s your case, investigator?”
